title: Indian Startup Astrobase Wins Government Backing to Build SpaceX-Style Rocket Engine, Targets 2029 Orbital Launch
excerpt: Bengaluru-based Astrobase is developing an 800 kN full-flow staged combustion engine — the same architecture that powers SpaceX's Raptor — with IN-SPACe funding and a test facility already running hot-fire tests.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Astrobase is developing an 800 kN reusable rocket engine with government funding.
  • The engine features full-flow staged combustion, similar to SpaceX's Raptor.
  • Hot-fire tests are ongoing, with a 2029 orbital launch planned.
  • India aims for a $44 billion space economy by 2034, with Astrobase as a key player.

IN-SPACe funding announcement
  • Astrobase Space Technologies has been selected by IN-SPACe for funding under the Technology Adoption Fund to develop an 800 kN-class reusable LOX-methane rocket engine.
  • The engine uses full-flow staged combustion — the same cycle as SpaceX's Raptor, making it potentially the most advanced rocket engine developed in India's private sector.
  • Hot-fire testing is underway at Astrobase's propulsion test facility in Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh, with a maiden orbital launch targeted for 2029.
  • India aims to build a $44 billion space economy by 2034, and Astrobase is one of three startups selected in IN-SPACe's first round of TAF funding.

In a propulsion test facility in Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh, a rocket engine is being put through its paces that represents something India's space sector has never attempted before. Astrobase Space Technologies, a Bengaluru-based startup founded in 2024 by former ISRO engineers and industry veterans, is building a full-flow staged combustion engine — the most thermodynamically efficient rocket engine cycle ever devised, and the same architecture that powers SpaceX's Raptor engines on the Starship vehicle.

The Indian government has now put money behind the bet. IN-SPACe, the agency responsible for promoting private participation in India's space sector, selected Astrobase as one of three startups in the inaugural round of its Technology Adoption Fund. The grant agreement, linked to defined technical milestones, was signed by Astrobase co-founder and CEO Neeraj Khandelwal at a ceremony attended by Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal.

Why This Engine Matters

"Full-scale engine trials are scheduled for 2026, with a maiden orbital launch targeted for 2029.</p> <blockquote class="pull-quote"> <p>"Scaling up technology also would require money."

Full-flow staged combustion, or FFSC, is rocket engineering's most demanding propulsion cycle. In a conventional engine, either the fuel or the oxidizer runs through a single preburner before entering the main combustion chamber. In an FFSC engine, both fuel and oxidizer are routed through separate preburners, ensuring that everything entering the main chamber is already gasified and at optimal temperature. The result is higher efficiency, lower thermal stress, and — critically — the ability to reuse the engine across multiple flights.

Until recently, only two entities had successfully demonstrated FFSC: the Soviet Union's experimental RD-270 program in the 1960s, and SpaceX with its Raptor engine. Astrobase is building an 800 kN-class engine running on liquid oxygen and methane — the same propellant combination SpaceX chose for Raptor and which the industry has broadly converged on as the fuel of the future for reusable rockets.

The company completed a successful sub-scale hot-fire test in September 2025, validating combustion stability, materials, and flow systems. Full-scale engine trials are scheduled for 2026, with a maiden orbital launch targeted for 2029.

"Scaling up technology also would require money. We need to have more and more investments coming in domestically, internationally, whether in the form of philanthropy, from foundations, from business players."

— Jitendra Singh, Union Minister of State for Science and Technology

Building the Infrastructure In-House

What distinguishes Astrobase from many space startups — in India and globally — is the degree to which it has built its infrastructure domestically. The company operates a 46,000-square-foot assembly factory in Bengaluru and India's first private high-thrust LOX-LNG rocket engine test facility in Anantapur, approved in early 2025.

The engine is designed to power a reusable medium-lift launch vehicle with a four-meter-diameter booster employing seven engines in a configuration reminiscent of SpaceX's Falcon 9. The first stage is engineered for recovery and reuse, addressing a critical bottleneck in India's launch capabilities: the country currently relies on ISRO's PSLV and GSLV for orbital missions, and capacity has struggled to keep pace with the explosion in satellite constellation demand.

A $44 Billion Ambition

Astrobase's funding comes alongside two other IN-SPACe selections: SatSure Analytics, which will build Dhaarini, an AI-powered Earth observation foundation model; and TM2SPACE Technologies, developing AI-enabled star tracker systems for satellites. Together, the three companies represent the agency's first concrete investment in closing technology gaps in propulsion, observation, and navigation.

The selection follows a year-long multi-stage evaluation by an expert committee comprising representatives from ISRO, DPIIT, DST, academia, and industry. IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka said the initiative aims to "bridge the gap between early-stage development and commercial deployment, enabling Indian companies to build globally competitive space solutions."

India has set an ambitious target of building a $44 billion space economy by 2034. The country's private space sector has already produced Skyroot Aerospace, which recently became the first Indian private company to complete an orbital launch. Astrobase is attempting something more technically audacious: building the propulsion system that could make Indian rockets competitive with SpaceX on reusability and cost — a challenge no other Indian private company has publicly undertaken.
